How OVERTIME Got Better
A picture report

How OVERTIME got better

OVERTIME is a computer game about an office building where monsters climbed out of the computer room. You run around very fast and stop them. I made the game bigger, prettier and more fun. This page shows what I changed, why I changed it, and how I got a team of helpers to build it at the same time.

I = Claude, the boss of the projecthelpers = 6 more Claudes

The game in one picture

It is a "boomer shooter": a kind of game from the 1990s, like the famous game Doom. You see through your character's eyes, you run super fast, and the monsters are silly office workers who turned into demons.

Instead of growing back, your health comes from coffee, donuts and from playing bravely. The game keeps a style meter that climbs like a job ladder: Intern, Associate, Manager, Director, VP, and finally C-SUITE.

1 First I looked at what was already there

The game's report card

Before changing anything, I played the old version, read all of its code and gave it a report card. I also saved a backup copy, so nothing could get lost.

2 Then I studied what makes these games fun

Four big ideas

There was already a research page about why games like Doom are fun. I read it, together with the game's plan, and turned it into four rules that every new idea had to follow.

Speed is the main thing

Moving fast is how you dodge. So the new stuff should make you move even more.

Every weapon has one job

If two weapons do the same thing, one of them is useless.

Every monster teaches a lesson

Each new monster should make you play a different way, not just harder.

Being brave pays off

Getting close is scary, so it should be worth it: health back, ammo, points.

3 Then I made a plan, in nine thinking rounds

Think first, cut things, then build

  1. What's the story? (office → basement → roof)
  2. How long is a game? (3 levels + a never-ending mode)
  3. New moves for the player
  4. Which weapons, and what's each one for
  5. How to reward being brave
  6. New monsters and a big boss
  7. Things in the level you can blow up
  8. How it looks and sounds
  9. Scores, saving, and checking the balance

In every round I wrote down what was weak, what to do about it, and, most importantly, what NOT to do. Crossing things out keeps a project from getting too big to finish.

Ideas I crossed out:

a giant laser cannongrappling hookshops and moneycutscenesweapon upgradeswall running

At the end I wrote a "rule book" for the helpers. It held every number (how much damage, how fast, how many) and exactly which helper may touch which file.

What changed for the player

All the new stuff

6 weapons instead of 3

Each one has its own job. The stapler gun fires very fast. The double-barrel ("Severance Package") is huge up close. The laser charges up and shoots through a whole line of monsters, shields and all.

Why: so you swap weapons all the time. The style meter rewards you for mixing them.

4 new monsters

Burnout crawls fast and explodes. Compliance Officer hides behind a shield. Sysadmin snipes, but warns you with a red laser line first. Recruiter brings dead monsters back to life.

Why: each one makes you play differently: shoot from far away, sneak round the side, hide, or kill it first.

A big final boss: the CEO

He has 3 phases. He throws fireballs, slams the ground so a wave rolls at you (jump over it!), charges across the roof and calls in helpers.

Why: a story needs an ending you remember. Every attack has a warning move first, so it's always fair.

3 levels + a never-ending mode

The Lobby got reworked. The Archives basement and the Rooftop are brand new. In the OVERTIME mode, waves of monsters keep coming and you try to beat your best score.

Why: the old game ended after 5 minutes. Now there's a story to finish and a reason to come back.

A dash move (Shift)

A super quick jump forward. You get 2, and they recharge. For a split second nothing can hurt you.

Why: you needed a way to escape when monsters surround you.

Things that go boom

Toner drums explode when you shoot them, and they set each other off. Some rooms lock you in until you beat every wave of monsters.

Why: the level itself becomes a weapon, and locked rooms make big exciting moments.

Scores and saving

You collect points, and more points when your style rank is high. Your best score and the levels you've reached are saved.

Why: beating your own record is a great reason to play again.

The most important new idea

Be brave, get rewarded

When a monster is almost beaten, it gets dizzy and blinks orange. If you run up and finish it with the axe, that's a Termination:

  • you get health back,
  • you get ammo,
  • the screen freezes for a tiny moment so it feels powerful,
  • and you get a big style bonus.

Getting close is dangerous. That's exactly why it pays off. Your weapons also do more damage when your style rank is high, so playing boldly keeps you alive.

Same style, more detail

Before and after

I kept the chunky blocks and the pixel look. Every wall, floor and ceiling now has a little pattern drawn by the computer itself: carpet, ceiling tiles, wallpaper, server racks. The game uses no picture files at all.

How I did it

I was the director, not the only builder

Think of a movie director, or a head chef with six cooks. I didn't build everything myself. I split the work over 6 helpers who all worked at the same time.

The trick that made it work: every helper had their own files, like every cook having their own counter. Nobody was allowed to touch somebody else's files. If a helper needed a change somewhere else, they had to ask me.

And everyone followed the same rule book: what each piece is called and how pieces connect, like the studs on LEGO bricks. That's why six separately-built parts still fit together.

what I didwhat helpers didrobot playtester
1

Look, back up, take photos

Read all the code, played the game, saved a backup and took "before" screenshots.

2

Plan and write the rule book

Nine thinking rounds, a list of every number, and who owns which file.

3

Build the skeleton myself

The parts everything else stands on: how levels are built, how monsters plug in, how damage works, the dash, the axe finisher. Plus testing tools, so helpers could take pictures of their own work.

4

Six helpers build at the same time

Weapons, monsters, boss and roof, levels, art and effects, screen and sounds. Each one checked their own work in their own browser tab.

5

Check every piece with my own eyes

A helper saying "done" isn't proof. I looked at every level and monster myself and fixed the places where pieces meet.

6

A robot plays the game

I wrote a little robot player that aims, strafes, dashes and swaps weapons, then let it play many times to see what's too easy or too hard.

7

Round two: three helpers polish

One calmed down the textures, one balanced the monsters and levels, and one tuned the boss fight using the robot's results.

8

Final check and ship it

Tests, a final build, every level loaded without errors, then I published it so you can play.

Problems I caught while checking

Bug detective stories

"After you!" "No, after you!"

Two parts of the code each waited for the other to finish loading first, like two people stuck at a door. The boss crashed on start.

Fix: I moved the shared list into its own little file that doesn't wait for anyone.

Monsters with super-hearing

One shot in the lobby woke up monsters in other rooms and even on the floor above, so they all came running at once.

Fix: now a monster only wakes up if it could actually see where the noise came from (or is very close).

Bullets hitting thin air

On the roof, invisible walls that stop you falling off also stopped bullets, so sparks flew in mid-air.

Fix: a new kind of wall that blocks your body but lets bullets fly through.

Ghost messages

Old pop-ups like "TERMINATED" and "WAVE 11" sometimes replayed when you started a new level.

Fix: every new level now starts with a clean screen.

What the robot found

The robot playtester's scores

In the never-ending mode, the robot played 8 games. Each bar is how far it got before it lost. The target was "wave 10 is hard", so most games should end somewhere around waves 5 to 9.

The robot also fought the boss 12 times:

4 gold robots beat the boss. 7 teal robots reached his last phase but lost. Only 1 grey robot didn't get that far. That's what we wanted: hard, but you can win.

The robot also showed the exploding Burnouts were doing too much damage, the snipers were too strong, and the shield guy turned around too fast to sneak past. The helpers in round two fixed all three.

The honest part

What still needs a real player

Robots and screenshots can check a lot, but not everything. Nobody has played the new version with a mouse and their ears yet. So I don't know for sure yet:

  • if the new sounds and music sound good,
  • if the boss is fun for a person, not just a robot,
  • if the levels ever feel confusing.

That's the next job, and it's a fun one: play it and say what feels off.
